summary: Materials consumed, under Canada's federal SR&ED program, are physical inputs destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials carried out in Canada. 1. Executive Summary and Macro-Fiscal Architecture

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive landscape is anchored by the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which stands as the largest single source of federal government support for industrial innovation in the country. During the 2024–2025 fiscal year, the program delivered $4.5 billion in investment tax credits (ITCs) across more than 22,000 processed claims supporting over 19,000 claiming enterprises. By the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) reported $4.9 billion in investment tax credits claimed and $4.6 billion allowed, representing an expansion of roughly 50% in annual credit value since fiscal year 2022 and supporting approximately 24,160 businesses annually. Rather than winding down or ceding ground to discretionary industrial subsidies, the SR&ED program functions as an expanding, entitlement-based pillar of Canadian fiscal and innovation policy.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax architecture underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade. Following a two-phase national consultation initiated by the Department of Finance Canada in January 2024 and policy announcements in Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) and the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Applicable retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, raising the maximum annual refundable federal cash credit from $1.05 million to $2.10 million. Simultaneously, the legislation widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time via a three-year average gross revenue test, and reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs acquired after December 15, 2024.

At the sub-national level, provincial governments have similarly restructured their R&D tax regimes to align with evolving capital intensity and commercialization timelines. Most notably, Québec abolished five legacy R&D tax credit programs—including its longstanding R&D wage tax credit on Form RD-1029.7—for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the unified Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), which broadens eligible expenditures to encompass capital property and downstream pre-commercialization activities. When federal SR&ED incentives are stacked with provincial tax credits in jurisdictions such as Ontario, Québec, Alberta, British Columbia, and Atlantic Canada, alongside targeted non-dilutive programs such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and the $300 million AI Compute Access Fund, Canadian enterprises can recover between 42% and 65% of qualifying R&D expenditures.

Despite persistent industry perceptions that SR&ED audits are prohibitively adversarial, empirical CRA administrative data for the 2025–2026 reporting cycle reveals that 90% of SR&ED claims were accepted as filed, an additional 6% were accepted following audit modifications, and only 4% were denied entirely. This 96% overall allowance rate indicates that compliance failures stem overwhelmingly from post-hoc narrative reconstruction, improper cloud and overhead accounting under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rules, or missed statutory deadlines under subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act, rather than institutional unwillingness to disburse credits.

body.text: 2. Statutory & Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
2.1 Dual-Pillar Structure Under the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED tax incentive program operates through a bifurcated statutory mechanism embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Rather than functioning as a discretionary government grant, SR&ED is a statutory entitlement governed by two distinct but interlocking legislative pillars: the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) investment tax credit.

The first pillar is the Subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Under general income computation principles in subsection 9(1) and paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA, business expenses are deductible only to the extent they are incurred for the purpose of gaining or producing income from a business or property, while paragraph 18(1)(b) prohibits the deduction of outlays on account of capital. Because experimental R&D frequently generates enduring intangible capital assets or spans multi-year pre-revenue phases, subsection 37(1) overrides paragraph 18(1)(b) by establishing a dedicated pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures for work carried on in Canada. Within this pool, paragraph 37(1)(a) captures current expenditures on SR&ED, while the newly restored paragraph 37(1)(b) captures eligible capital expenditures. Taxpayers may elect to deduct any portion of their available subsection 37(1) pool in the current taxation year to reduce net business income for tax purposes, or they may defer the deduction and carry unclaimed pool balances forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future profitable years.

The second pillar is the Subsection 127(9) Investment Tax Credit (ITC) and Section 127.1 Refundability Framework. Once an expenditure qualifies for inclusion in the subsection 37(1) pool—or is calculated as a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in lieu of itemized overhead under ITR subsection 2900(4)—it enters the computation of "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Subsection 127(5) permits the resulting SR&ED ITC to be deducted directly against federal Part I income tax otherwise payable, while section 127.1 governs the cash refundability of unused ITCs for qualifying corporations and unincorporated taxpayers.

A critical structural mechanism connects these two pillars across sequential taxation years through mandatory assistance and recapture adjustments. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9), any government assistance or non-government assistance—including provincial R&D tax credits and direct federal innovation grants—that a taxpayer receives, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing date reduces both the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base in the current taxation year. Furthermore, the federal SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in Year 1 (whether applied to offset Part I tax or received as a cash refund) reduces the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in Year 2 pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e). To the extent that the federal ITC claimed in Year 1 exceeds the remaining balance of the subsection 37(1) pool in Year 2—which routinely occurs when the taxpayer deducts the entire subsection 37(1) pool in Year 1 and also claims the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount that never entered the pool—the negative pool balance is included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA.
2.2 Legislative Evolution and Enactment of Bill C-15 (2024–2026)

The statutory parameters governing SR&ED filings in 2026 are the culmination of a multi-stage policy overhaul initiated in Budget 2022 to evaluate whether Canada's R&D tax framework remained globally competitive and effectively incentivized domestic intellectual property (IP) retention. On January 31, 2024, the Department of Finance Canada launched Phase One of formal public consultations on SR&ED modernization alongside parallel consultations on a potential Canadian patent box regime, both of which closed on April 15, 2024. Those consultations examined how to better support scaling R&D-intensive Canadian firms, whether to modernize the statutory definition and architecture of SR&ED, and how to retain IP ownership inside Canadian borders. On April 16, 2024, Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) committed $600 million over four years commencing in 2025—and $150 million annually on an ongoing basis—to enhance the SR&ED program, while launching Phase Two consultations running through May 27, 2024, to finalize technical reforms.

On December 13 and December 16, 2024, the Department of Finance released the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and accompanying policy backgrounders, followed by formal draft legislative proposals in early 2025. While the December 2024 FES initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% credit from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, subsequent federal fiscal commitments during the 2025 budget cycle expanded the annual expenditure cap further to $6.0 million. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, codifying these expansions into permanent law for all taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (with Budget 2026 proposing additional technical refinements to partnership and corporate threshold rules).
2.3 Enhanced vs. Basic Rates, Phase-Out Formulas, and Entity Eligibility
Under the enacted Bill C-15 regime, the rate and cash refundability of the federal SR&ED ITC depend on the taxpayer's legal classification, capital or revenue scale, and expenditure category.
Qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)

A corporation that qualifies throughout the taxation year as a CCPC under subsection 125(7) of the ITA is eligible to earn an enhanced 35% ITC under subsection 127(10.1) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual expenditure limit, which is now set at a maximum of $6,000,000. For a qualifying CCPC, the 35% ITC earned on current SR&ED expenditures up to the expenditure limit is 100% refundable, generating up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds even when the corporation has zero tax payable. Conversely, the 35% ITC earned on newly eligible capital SR&ED expenditures up to the expenditure limit is partially refundable at a rate of 40% (yielding an immediate 14% effective cash refund on capital spend, with the remaining 60% of the credit available to offset Part I tax or carry forward). Qualified expenditures (both current and capital) exceeding the CCPC's annual expenditure limit earn the basic 15% ITC, which is generally non-refundable unless the CCPC meets the "qualifying corporation" criteria where prior-year taxable income does not exceed its qualifying income limit, in which case the 15% credit is 40% refundable.

Prior to Bill C-15, a CCPC's $3.0 million expenditure limit was reduced under subsection 127(10.2) if its taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3, sections 181.2 to 181.4 of the ITA, aggregated across all associated corporations) for the preceding taxation year lay between $10 million and $50 million. Under Bill C-15, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds are raised to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, while corresponding increases apply to the taxable capital phase-out thresholds used to determine a CCPC's qualifying income limit for partial refundability. The statutory expenditure limit formula for a CCPC (or associated group) under the taxable capital test is expressed as:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000

In this formula, A represents the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year, with the resulting limit prorated for short taxation years of fewer than 365 days. When aggregate prior-year taxable capital reaches or exceeds $75,000,000, the expenditure limit drops to nil, and the CCPC earns no refundable ITC at all, reverting to the non-refundable 15% ITC on all SR&ED expenditures. Crucially, Bill C-15 also introduces an elective revenue-based alternative for CCPCs: a CCPC may elect to have its annual expenditure limit determined based on the corporation's (or associated group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years rather than prior-year taxable capital. This election prevents capital-intensive clean-technology, biomanufacturing, semiconductor, and hardware scale-ups with substantial debt or preferred equity on their balance sheets from being prematurely ground down out of the 35% refundable tier while still in pre-revenue or early commercialization stages.
Extension to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, when a high-growth Canadian technology or life sciences enterprise completed an initial public offering (IPO) or listed on a designated stock exchange such as the TSX or TSX Venture Exchange, it ceased to be a CCPC and immediately forfeited access to the 35% refundable SR&ED rate, dropping to the 15% non-refundable rate regardless of whether it generated taxable income. Bill C-15 eliminates this structural penalty against public listings by extending the 35% refundable ITC up to the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must be resident in Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected/been designated to be a public corporation), and not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons.

Because public corporations routinely carry large share capital balances that would distort a Part I.3 taxable capital calculation, an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based on the corporation's (or its consolidated accounting group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years ending before the current taxation year:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − B) ÷ $60,000,000], where B is nil if average annual gross revenue is $15,000,000 or less and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average revenue exceeds $15,000,000

Mirroring the CCPC rules, an ECPC receives 100% refundability on the 35% ITC earned on current expenditures and 40% refundability on the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures up to its expenditure limit, while qualified expenditures in excess of the limit earn the non-refundable 15% ITC.
Other Corporations, Partnerships, Individuals, and Trusts

Foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries (such as Canadian R&D centres of U.S., European, or Asian multinationals), public corporations controlled by non-residents, and domestic corporations exceeding the $75 million taxable capital or revenue threshold earn the basic 15% non-refundable ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures without an upper expenditure cap. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I income tax payable.

Unincorporated businesses, sole proprietors, individuals, and certain trusts earn the basic 15% ITC, which is partially refundable at a rate of 40% (yielding an effective 6% cash refund after applying credits against Part I tax payable). Where SR&ED is carried out by a partnership, the partnership is a flow-through entity that cannot retain a subsection 37(1) expenditure pool; all current SR&ED expenditures must be deducted at the partnership level in computing partnership net income in the fiscal period incurred, and the resulting 15% ITC is allocated to the qualifying partners at year-end (excluding limited partners or passive "specified members"), where it is generally non-refundable. Consequently, corporate tax advisors strongly recommend incorporating R&D operations into a CCPC prior to incurring substantial R&D costs to capture the 35% fully refundable credit and the indefinite subsection 37(1) pool carryforward.
Associated Corporation Rules and Subsection 127(10.3) Allocations

Where two or more corporations are "associated" in a taxation year under section 256 of the ITA—encompassing de jure voting control, de facto control in fact under subsection 256(5.1), cross-ownership rules, and non-arm's-length family attribution—the entire associated group must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and aggregate their prior-year taxable capital or three-year average revenue across all associated entities worldwide. The associated corporations must execute and file an annual allocation agreement under subsection 127(10.3) (using Schedule T2SCH49) to apportion the shared expenditure limit among the group before any member claims the enhanced 35% rate. Ignoring the association rules in venture-backed holdco/opco structures or sister-company arrangements is a primary trigger for CRA reassessment.
3. Scientific & Technological Eligibility Criteria and Jurisprudence
3.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1)

The substantive gateway to both the section 37 deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (formerly housed in section 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations). Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four permitted statutory categories.

The first category, under paragraph 248(1)(a), is Basic Research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; because basic research is predominantly conducted inside universities and foundational research institutes, it represents the smallest fraction of corporate SR&ED claims. The second category, under paragraph 248(1)(b), is Applied Research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and vastly predominant category—accounting for over 90% of corporate claims in Canada—is Experimental Development under paragraph 248(1)(c), defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The fourth category, under paragraph 248(1)(d), covers Support Work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but only where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) establish an explicit statutory boundary by excluding seven categories of commercial and routine engineering activity from SR&ED regardless of industry: market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
3.2 The CRA Three-Question Framework vs. The Judicial Five-Question Test

In administering subsection 248(1) during technical reviews, the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development evaluate every claimed project through three sequential eligibility questions that must all be answered in the affirmative. First, the CRA asks whether there was a scientific or technological uncertainty—specifically, whether the technical problem or system constraint could be resolved using standard engineering, publicly available knowledge, or routine methodologies accessible to competent professionals in the field. Second, the CRA examines whether the effort involved systematic investigation or search, requiring the claimant to formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty and to test those hypotheses through planned experimentation, observation, and analysis rather than ad hoc troubleshooting. Third, the CRA evaluates whether the overall approach was aimed at achieving a scientific or technological advancement, meaning the generation of new technological knowledge or capability that advances the underlying state of technology, even if the advancement is incremental or the experiment fails to achieve its commercial objective.

These three administrative questions are distilled directly from the binding five-question legal test established by Justice Donald Bowman in the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998, 98 DTC 1839; [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520) and subsequently adopted as the governing law of Canada by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 CanLII 8879 (FCA)) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393). Under Canadian tax jurisprudence, every SR&ED project is adjudicated against these five cumulative criteria:

First, under Question 1 (Technological Risk or Uncertainty), the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Justice Bowman defined "routine engineering" as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant scientific or technological field. If the uncertainty concerns only whether a product will be commercially accepted by customers (market uncertainty) or whether a known architectural approach can be implemented within time or budget constraints, no technological uncertainty exists. For example, in software engineering, not knowing whether a specific algorithm can process 10 million events per second with sub-100-millisecond latency on commodity hardware due to memory-bus contention or algorithmic scaling limits represents a true technological uncertainty, whereas integrating third-party APIs or debugging routine code does not.

Second, under Question 2 (Hypothesis Formulation), the court asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. In Northwest Hydraulic, the Tax Court articulated a five-stage methodology that characterizes this stage: (a) the observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) the formulation of a clear technological objective; (c) the identification and articulation of the specific technological uncertainty; (d) the formulation of an hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) the methodical and systematic testing of those hypotheses.

Third, under Question 3 (Accordance with the Scientific Method), the court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. While intuition and engineering creativity may spark the initial hypothesis, the investigation itself must be characterized by trained and systematic observation, quantitative measurement, and experiment, clearly distinguishing the effort from random trial and error.

Fourth, under Question 4 (Technological Advancement), the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Crucially, the jurisprudence confirms that "technological advancement" is synonymous with gaining new knowledge that advances the general understanding of the technology to a level beyond what was publicly available or known to competent professionals at the outset of the project. An advancement may be incremental, and the decisive rejection of an hypothesis because an experimental prototype fails still constitutes a valid technological advancement because it proves why a given technical approach cannot work under specific boundary conditions.

Fifth, under Question 5 (Contemporaneous Record-Keeping), the court asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the experimental results was kept as the work progressed. As confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Canafric Inc. v. The King and Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King (2026 FCA 175), contemporaneous records generated during the R&D execution phase are the primary evidentiary mechanism by which a taxpayer proves that the scientific method was actually followed.
3.3 Authoritative Case Law and Audit Precedents

A rigorous audit defence requires an exact command of how the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) apply the Northwest Hydraulic criteria to contested claims. In reviewing the jurisprudence, practitioners must also correct a frequent citation error in secondary tax literature: the widely cited theatrical rigging decision is officially indexed as Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (not 2017 TCC 88). In Joel Theatrical Rigging, the claimant attempted to develop a silent, heavy-duty counterweight rigging brake and a slow-descent theatrical curtain system. The Tax Court dismissed the appeal because the claimant failed to formulate testable hypotheses or take basic quantitative measurements during trials—such as measuring the exact weight of the curtain, the duration of the trials, or the rate of the curtain's descent—holding that unmeasured adjustments amounted to random "trial and error" rather than systematic observation, measurement, and experiment under the scientific method.

Similarly, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261), Justice D'Arcy emphasized the independence of each Northwest Hydraulic criterion: although the taxpayer provided sufficient documentation proving it had conducted a structured, "systematic investigation," the appeal was dismissed because the underlying engineering problems did not involve true technological risk or advancement beyond routine engineering. Conversely, in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1816, TCC 1998), Justice Archambault clarified that while contemporaneous written reports are the gold standard under Question 5, neither the Income Tax Act nor the Regulations make written reports an absolute statutory condition precedent to claiming section 37 expenditures; credible, detailed oral testimony can be adduced to substantiate SR&ED where documentary records are incomplete, though subsequent appellate rulings in RIS-Christie, Canafric, and Tuna Temple demonstrate that relying on oral testimony without contemporaneous data logs carries severe litigation risk.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods, and Cloud/Capital Cost Rules

Once a project satisfies the scientific eligibility criteria of subsection 248(1), only specific categories of expenditures incurred in Canada qualify for the subsection 37(1) pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC.
4.1 Salaries and Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary expenditure base for most claimants. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, employee time is categorized into direct hands-on technical execution (such as running experiments, writing experimental code, or analysing test data) and first-line technical supervision that directly guides the experimental direction, plus a portion of directly supporting technical staff time. General administrative management, human resources, finance, and clerical tasks are excluded from direct SR&ED wages and are instead captured either via the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount or as directly attributable incremental overhead under the Traditional Method. Every dollar of claimed salary must be supported by contemporaneous time tracking that codes employee hours by project between SR&ED-qualifying and non-qualifying commercial tasks.

A narrow statutory exception exists under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) and the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy for SR&ED performed outside Canada: permissible salaries and wages paid to an employee who is a resident of Canada for SR&ED work performed physically outside Canada are eligible only if the foreign work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of SR&ED carried on by the taxpayer inside Canada, and the total foreign SR&ED wages claimed cannot exceed 10% of the total salaries and wages paid for SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year.
Restrictions on "Specified Employees" (Connected Shareholders)

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" of a corporation is an employee who is a specified shareholder—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to it—or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse, child, parent, or sibling of a 10%+ shareholder). To prevent owner-managers from inflating SR&ED refunds via discretionary year-end bonus declarations, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose three strict statutory caps on specified employees.

First, for any specified employee, the SR&ED salary base completely excludes all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits (including employee stock option benefits under section 7 of the ITA, which are never deductible for corporate tax or SR&ED purposes), and unpaid remuneration from a prior year paid in the current year (reported on line 310 of Form T661 pursuant to subsection 78(4), which disallows any accrued salary that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred). Second, the maximum direct SR&ED salary claimable for a specified employee in a taxation year is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed in the year. Third, under subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, the amount of a specified employee's salary that can be included in the salary base to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total base salary or wages (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, after excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages) or 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for the number of days of employment in the taxation year according to the statutory formula in ITR subsection 2900(7):
Maximum PPA salary base = lesser of (75% × A) and (2.5 × B × C ÷ 365)

In this formula, A is the specified employee's eligible base salary across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED activities, B is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, and C is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for the portion of the year during which the individual was not a specified employee, and with mandatory aggregation across associated corporations under ITR subsection 2900(8)).
4.2 Overhead Election: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers must elect annually on Form T661 (Part 3, Section A) to calculate SR&ED overhead and other expenditures using either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that year.
The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) – Statutory Rate Correction (55%, Not 65%)

Under the Proxy Method (governed by subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations), instead of tracking, itemizing, and apportioning actual SR&ED overhead expenses, the taxpayer calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (including directly engaged wages and eligible administrative salary or wages under ITR subsection 2900(5), subject to the subsection 2900(7) specified employee caps and subsection 2900(9) exclusions).

A critical audit verification point must be underscored: certain defective commercial summaries and automated advisories erroneously state that the PPA provides "a fixed overhead rate of about 65% of direct salaries for 2026 filings". In point of law, the PPA rate under ITR subsection 2900(4) was 65% only for taxation years ending in 2012 and earlier; following the enactment of Bill C-45 (Jobs and Growth Act, 2012, S.C. 2012, c. 31), the rate stepped down to 60% for the 2013 calendar year and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014 (as confirmed in the CRA's revised Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, which formally deleted all historical references to 60% and 65% on April 28, 2022). Filing a claim using a 65% proxy rate overstates the notional overhead by 10 percentage points and results in an automatic reduction on CRA assessment.

Furthermore, the PPA is strictly a notional amount included in "qualified expenditure" under paragraph (b) of the definition in subsection 127(9) for the sole purpose of computing the SR&ED ITC. The PPA is not added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual underlying overhead outlays (such as office rent, utilities, general supplies, and indirect support costs) are deducted in the ordinary course of business under subsection 9(1) and paragraph 18(1)(a).
The Traditional Method

Under the Traditional Method (governed by subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) to (III) of the ITA), the taxpayer foregoes the 55% notional proxy and instead itemizes and justifies actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (meaning costs that are directly related and incremental to the SR&ED work, and would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not occurred). Unlike the PPA, actual overhead claimed under the Traditional Method is added to both the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC base.

body.text: 4.3 Cloud Computing, Hosting, and AI Infrastructure Costs

For modern software-as-a-service (SaaS), data analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI) companies, the tax treatment of cloud computing infrastructure (such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and dedicated GPU compute clusters) represents one of the highest-risk audit areas.

First, claimants must navigate the Proxy vs. Traditional Method trap for cloud costs. A widespread compliance error occurs when claimants elect the Proxy Method (claiming the 55% PPA on salaries) and simultaneously attempt to claim cloud hosting or software subscription invoices that constitute overhead. Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead is not identified at all because the 55% PPA statutorily stands in for all overhead and other expenditures; consequently, any cloud invoice characterized as overhead is disallowed in full if claimed on top of the PPA. Choosing between the Proxy and Traditional methods is therefore an exercise in arithmetic modelling rather than a default assumption. For a team of five engineers with $600,000 of eligible SR&ED salary, the Proxy Method yields $330,000 of notional overhead ($600,000 × 55%). If that same team is conducting compute-heavy AI model training where incremental SR&ED cloud compute bills exceed $330,000, electing the Traditional Method allows the company to itemize and claim 100% of its actual incremental SR&ED cloud overhead in both the section 37 pool and the ITC base.

Second, claimants must enforce mandatory segregation of production (COGS) vs. experimental R&D environments. Under both ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises) and CRA audit guidelines, cloud infrastructure used for live customer production (Cost of Goods Sold / Cost of Revenue), commercial payment processing (e.g., Stripe or PayPal fees), production third-party API calls, staging environments used for routine quality assurance testing, or general business operations is strictly ineligible for SR&ED. SaaS and AI claimants must configure cloud resource tags in AWS, GCP, or Azure from Day 1 to separate "production" accounts (coded to COGS) from "sred-experimental" development accounts, attributing specific cloud compute expenditures to specific Form T661 project codes and Git commit logs.

Third, prepaid cloud and software commitments are restricted by subsection 18(9) of the ITA. Where a company pays upfront for multi-year or annual committed cloud bandwidth, support contracts, or software subscriptions that extend beyond the fiscal year-end, subsection 18(9) restricts current-year deductibility to the portion of services actually rendered within the taxation year, requiring the prepaid balance to be scheduled and amortized into the subsequent period.
4.4 Subcontractors, Materials, and University/Research Institute Payments

Payments to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors performing SR&ED on behalf of the claimant are 100% deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in "qualified expenditure" when calculating the subsection 127(9) ITC. This statutory 20% reduction removes the subcontractor's presumed profit margin from the tax credit base. To qualify, the contracted work must be performed physically within Canada by the subcontractor, and the statement of work and vendor invoices must tie the expenditure to a specific SR&ED project, vendor, and date. Where work is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length contractor (such as a sister corporation owned by the same shareholders), the 80% rule does not apply; instead, the claimant's qualified expenditure is restricted to the non-arm's-length contractor's actual underlying SR&ED expenditures rather than the amount invoiced. Furthermore, payments to non-resident contractors for R&D performed outside Canada are ineligible for SR&ED, and any payment to a non-resident contractor for services rendered physically in Canada is subject to a mandatory 15% withholding tax under section 105 of the Income Tax Regulations, while cross-border payments for rents, royalties, and similar amounts attract a 25% withholding tax under Part XIII of the ITA unless reduced by treaty. Similarly, payments made to approved Canadian universities, colleges, or research institutes for SR&ED related to the claimant's business class are included in the federal ITC base at 80%.

For physical inputs, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada is 100% eligible for both the section 37 pool and the section 127(9) ITC. Materials are "consumed" when they are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials, whereas materials are "transformed" when they are incorporated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant. However, if a transformed material or experimental prototype is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED Recapture Rules (subsections 127(27) to (35) of the ITA, with parallel provincial recapture in Alberta) claw back the ITC previously claimed on the lesser of the original cost of the property and its fair market value or proceeds of disposition, adding the recaptured credit directly to the corporation's tax otherwise payable.
4.5 Reinstated Capital Expenditures and Accelerated CCA Regimes (2024–2033)

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property) and capital lease costs were completely excluded from SR&ED. Bill C-15 restores pre-2014 capital expenditure eligibility for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024)—and for lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024—to both the subsection 37(1) SR&ED income deduction and the 15% or 35% SR&ED ITCs. This reinstatement allows AI, clean-tech, biomanufacturing, and hardware companies acquiring dedicated on-premise GPU servers, laboratory apparatus, or testing equipment to claim both a 100% current-year deduction and the 35% ITC (which is partially refundable at a rate of 40% on capital expenditures for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs).

For capital assets that are used in general R&D or commercial operations outside the SR&ED capital rules, deductibility is governed by the Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) regime under paragraph 20(1)(a) of the ITA and section 1100 and Schedule II of the Income Tax Regulations (since paragraph 18(1)(b) denies immediate deduction of capital outlays, while SaaS and cloud-hosted tools remain current operating expenses under paragraph 18(1)(a)). Practitioners should note that there is no statutory rule requiring hardware to be used "over 50% for work" before it can be depreciated; CCA is claimed on the exact business-use percentage of the capital cost (for instance, 40% business use supports CCA on 40% of the cost), and closed classes such as Class 52 accept no new additions. Under Budget 2024 and Bill C-15, two overlapping accelerated depreciation regimes operate concurrently depending on when the property is acquired and when it becomes available for use (while prohibiting double-dipping on the same dollar between SR&ED and CCA):

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive: Ontario's Dual-Credit Interaction and Multiplicative Phase-Out

Ontario operates two main corporate SR&ED tax credits that layer simultaneously onto the same pool of Ontario-incurred SR&ED expenditures, alongside the specialized 20% refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, capped at $20 million of qualified expenditures per associated group).

A rigorous fact-check of Ontario's statutory rates is essential because unverified commercial blogs frequently misstate the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) at 20% or 12% and the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) at 10%. Under section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sch. A, and Ontario Regulation 37/09, for all taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016, the statutory rate for the OITC (Schedule 566) is strictly 8% refundable (down from 10% prior to June 1, 2016, as a 2018 budget proposal to introduce an R&D-intensity-based 12% rate was never enacted following a change in government), and the statutory rate for the ORDTC (Schedule 508) is strictly 3.5% non-refundable (down from 4.5% prior to June 1, 2016). Furthermore, the Government of Ontario has officially updated its OITC rules to mirror federal Bill C-15: a corporation's qualified expenditure in Ontario includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013, and before December 16, 2024, were excluded, and those made before January 1, 2014, were included at 40%).

The OITC's $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (which yields a maximum refundable credit of $240,000 per associated group) is reduced if the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (eliminated at $800,000) or if its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $25,000,000 (eliminated at $50,000,000). Crucially, under Schedule 566, if an associated group falls within both phase-out ranges simultaneously, the two surviving percentage ratios multiply together rather than taking the lesser of the two separate reductions:
OITC expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × [($800,000 − prior-year taxable income) ÷ $300,000] × [($50,000,000 − prior-year taxable capital) ÷ $25,000,000]

For instance, if an associated group has $700,000 of prior-year taxable income (leaving one-third of the $3.0M limit, or $1,000,000) and $37,500,000 of prior-year taxable capital (leaving 50% of the limit), the surviving OITC expenditure limit is $500,000 (generating a maximum OITC of $40,000), whereas erroneously taking the lesser of the two separate tests would have overstated the limit at $1,000,000.

In calculating the combined Ontario and federal credits, Ontario's legislation specifies a strict sequential grinding order. Under Ontario law, the OITC is expressly designated as government assistance for ORDTC purposes (whereas the ORDTC and the federal ITC do not reduce the OITC base when computing current-year entitlements on Schedule 566 and Schedule 508). Consequently, the 8% OITC is calculated first on the gross Ontario eligible expenditure pool; that 8% OITC entitlement is then subtracted from the Ontario expenditure pool to establish the net base multiplied by the 3.5% ORDTC rate (yielding a combined Ontario credit rate of 11.22%). Finally, both the 8% OITC and the 3.5% ORDTC constitute provincial government assistance for federal purposes under ITA subsection 127(9), reducing the expenditure base multiplied by the 35% (or 15%) federal ITC rate.

5.3 Deep-Dive: Québec's 2025–2026 Consolidation (The New CRIC Regime)

In its March 25, 2025 budget, the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive structural overhaul of its provincial R&D tax incentives, effective for taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025. Under this reform, Québec formally eliminated five legacy R&D tax credits for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025: the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium, and the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services (alongside the repeal of industrial design tax credits).

Replacing those five legacy credits is the unified Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) administered by Revenu Québec. Unlike the former RD-1029.7 regime—which was restricted to R&D salaries and subcontractor wages above an exclusion floor and phased down from 30% to 14% for corporations with worldwide assets between $50 million and $75 million—the new CRIC regime abolishes the exclusion threshold and expands eligibility in three major ways. First, it covers both traditional R&D and pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec in respect of the taxpayer's business (such as product certification, regulatory testing, industrial design, and pilot validation). Second, it broadens the eligible expenditure base to encompass salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to certain research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of property used in Québec R&D or pre-commercialization. Third, it provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures across an associated group and a 20% fully refundable rate on all excess eligible expenditures (with a flat 20% rate for a corporation that is a member of a qualified partnership, reported on lines 440p to 440y, codes 112 and 113 of Guide CO-17.G). Separately, for mineral resource development in Québec incurred after March 25, 2025, Québec amended its resource tax credit rates to 22.5% (or 45% for specific renewable/exploration categories) for non-operating members and 10% (or 20%) for operating members.
5.4 Deep-Dive: Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Following the expiration of the former Alberta SR&ED Tax Credit, the Government of Alberta introduced the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration under Information Circular IEG-1), applicable to eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020. Delivered directly through the Alberta corporate tax system without a pre-application process, eligible corporations claim the grant by filing AT1 Schedule 29 (alongside AT1 Schedule 16, Alberta Scientific Research Expenditures, and Form AT4970, Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (that is, 21 months after the end of the taxation year). Payments are disbursed once the qualifying expenditures have been verified by the CRA and confirmed to have been undertaken in Alberta by TRA.

The IEG provides a two-tier refundable credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta SR&ED spending (including the Alberta proxy amount), generating a maximum annual cash grant of $800,000. Specifically, the corporation earns an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to its "base level of spending"—calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years—and an enhanced 20% refundable payment on all eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds that two-year average base spending level:
IEG = (8% × lesser of eligible Alberta spending and base level of spending) + (20% × eligible Alberta spending in excess of the base level of spending)

Because a first-year R&D claimant or newly incorporated Alberta venture has a two-year prior spending average of zero, it earns the full 20% refundable rate on 100% of its eligible Alberta R&D spending up to $4.0 million in Year 1. The $4.0 million spending cap phases out linearly for corporations (and associated groups) with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital, and firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital (as well as partnerships, trusts, and individuals) are ineligible. Under federal ITA subsection 127(9), the Alberta IEG reduces the federal SR&ED deductible pool and qualified expenditure base in the year claimed.

PacifiCan RAII: $200K to $5.0M per project (up to 50% of eligible costs). ACOA RAII: Minimum $1.0M contribution. Delivered as interest-free repayable contributions.
Unconditionally repayable contributions are generally not government assistance unless forgiveness conditions exist; interest-free benefit may require technical review.
Clean Technology Manufacturing (CTM) ITC & Clean Tech / Clean Electricity ITCs
Taxable Canadian corporations investing in clean technology manufacturing machinery, critical mineral extraction (including polymetallic projects), or clean energy.
30% Refundable ITC on capital cost of eligible CTM machinery and equipment (15%–30% for Clean Tech / Clean Electricity ITCs).
Cannot claim both CTM ITC and SR&ED ITC on the exact same capital property dollar; requires strategic election between capital credits.
Alberta Innovates AICE & CanExport Innovation
AICE: Alberta tech validation and market access. CanExport: R&D collaboration with foreign partners.
AICE: Validate up to $300K; Market Access $300K–$600K (up to 75% of costs, 25% applicant share). CanExport: 75% of costs up to $37,500/project ($100K/yr cap).
Non-repayable grants reduce the SR&ED qualified expenditure base to the extent the funded costs are also SR&ED-eligible.

body.text: 6.2 Strategic Stacking Mechanics: NRC IRAP, AI Compute Access Fund, and SR&ED

While Canadian tax law strictly prohibits double-dipping (claiming the exact same unadjusted expenditure dollar under both a direct grant and SR&ED), properly structured "stacking" of direct grants with SR&ED substantially increases total non-dilutive recovery over claiming SR&ED alone.
The Proxy Method Multiplier When Stacking NRC IRAP and SR&ED

Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, when a CCPC receives an NRC IRAP contribution reimbursing a percentage of direct technical salaries, the IRAP grant constitutes government assistance under subsection 127(9) and reduces the pool of qualified expenditures. However, because the IRAP contribution reimburses only direct technical salaries and does not reimburse corporate overhead, the CCPC's 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under ITR subsection 2900(4) is still calculated on 100% of the gross eligible SR&ED salary base prior to deducting the IRAP grant.

To illustrate this statutory leverage, consider an Ontario CCPC with $100,000 in direct eligible SR&ED technical salaries that receives a 75% NRC IRAP grant ($75,000). First, the gross SR&ED salary base is $100,000, and the Prescribed Proxy Amount is $55,000, yielding $155,000 in pre-assistance qualified expenditures. Second, deducting the $75,000 NRC IRAP grant leaves $80,000 in net qualified expenditures (comprising $25,000 of unsubsidized salary plus the full $55,000 notional overhead proxy). Third, applying the 8% Ontario OITC ($6,400), the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC ($2,576), and the 35% federal SR&ED ITC ($24,858.40) generates $33,834.40 in combined SR&ED tax credits. Combined with the $75,000 NRC IRAP grant, the corporation recovers $108,834.40 (or 108.83% of its $100,000 direct payroll outlay, representing roughly 70.2% of its $155,000 total direct-plus-notional-overhead cost).
Stacking the AI Compute Access Fund with SR&ED and Scale AI

As part of Budget 2024's $2.4 billion artificial intelligence package—which included $2.0 billion for the Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy and AI Compute Access Fund, $200 million for regional AI adoption, $100 million for the NRC AI Assist Program, $50 million for affected workers, and funding for the AI Safety Institute of Canada—Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) administers the $300 million AI Compute Access Fund. Targeting Canadian-incorporated AI builders with fewer than 500 full-time equivalents (FTEs) who are training, fine-tuning, or running inference workloads (excluding pure API consumers, pre-funded ideation-stage startups, or projects below $100,000 in compute spend), the Access Fund reimburses up to two-thirds (~66.67%) of eligible cloud-based AI compute costs hosted in Canadian data centres and up to one-half (50%) of eligible non-Canadian cloud compute costs (with the non-Canadian fallback lane available only until March 31, 2027, when domestic capacity is unavailable or unsuitable) across project budgets of $100,000 to $5,000,000 running through March 31, 2028.

When stacking the AI Compute Access Fund, Scale AI, and SR&ED on the same underlying AI initiative, optimal tax compliance relies on strict line-item separation and reciprocal disclosure. If the AI builder elects the Proxy Method on Form T661, SR&ED claims the engineering labour and 55% PPA, while the AI Compute Access Fund claims the cloud GPU compute bills; because the two programs fund mutually exclusive cost categories, the Access Fund grant does not grind down the salary-based SR&ED ITC. Conversely, if the AI builder elects the Traditional Method (or claims compute as a consumed material) to include cloud compute on Form T661, the 66.67% or 50% Access Fund reimbursement must be netted off the SR&ED-eligible compute amount as government assistance. In all cases, the SR&ED Form T661 must disclose the Access Fund contribution and the Access Fund filing must disclose the SR&ED claim, as silence in either direction invites an immediate reassessment.
7. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Deadlines, and New CRA Audit Powers
7.1 Bicameral Governance and Required Tax Forms

Administration of the federal SR&ED program is divided between the Department of Finance Canada, which retains statutory responsibility for legislative policy under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers compliance, technical eligibility reviews, and financial audits. Within the CRA, claims are evaluated by two specialized cadres: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—domain engineers and scientists who evaluate whether claimed projects satisfy the subsection 248(1) criteria—and Financial Reviewers—tax auditors who verify salary bases, specified employee caps, overhead elections, subcontractor contracts, and government assistance grinds. (Where fast-growing companies face working-capital gaps prior to CRA disbursement, specialized private SR&ED lenders routinely advance 70% to 80% of the accrued credit at monthly interest rates of 1% to 2%, repaid upon CRA refund release).

To claim federal and provincial SR&ED incentives, a corporation must transmit its return electronically via Corporation Internet Filing using CRA-certified commercial tax software (note that EFILE is for third-party preparers and NETFILE is strictly for personal T1 returns) alongside its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. The mandatory filing package comprises Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, revised by the CRA in March 2026 to reflect Bill C-15), Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, or Form T2038(IND) for unincorporated taxpayers), Schedule T2SCH49 (for associated CCPC expenditure limit allocations under subsection 127(10.3)), and the applicable provincial schedules (such as Ontario Schedules 566, 508, and 568; BC Form T666; Manitoba Schedule 380; Saskatchewan Schedule 403; Nova Scotia Schedule 340; New Brunswick Schedule 360; Newfoundland and Labrador Schedule 301; Yukon Schedule 442; Alberta AT1 Schedules 29 and 16 and Form AT4970; and Revenu Québec CO-17 and RD forms). In Part 9 of Form T661, claimants and external advisors (who typically charge contingency fees of 15% to 25% of the refund or flat/automated software fees) must also disclose full claim preparer billing information under penalty of subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA.
7.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

One of the strictest statutory provisions in Canadian tax law is the SR&ED reporting deadline governed by subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Under paragraph 150(1)(a), a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year, and under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m), the taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule 31 containing all prescribed information within 12 months after the corporation's T2 filing due date.

Combining the 6-month T2 filing period with the additional 12-month SR&ED reporting period establishes an absolute statutory deadline of exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred (and this same strict 18-month deadline applies to provincial credits such as the Ontario OITC and ORDTC, except in Alberta where the IEG deadline is 15 months after the AT1 filing due date). For example, a corporation whose fiscal year ends on December 31, 2025, has an absolute SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2027. Crucially, there is no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion to extend the 18-month filing deadline; if Form T661 or Schedule 31 is filed even one day after the 18-month deadline, the expenditures are statutorily barred from the subsection 37(1) pool and the ITC is permanently lost.
7.3 Record Retention and Expanded CRA Audit Powers (Budget 2024 Enactments)

Under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the Income Tax Act, every taxpayer claiming SR&ED must retain all books of account, financial records, vendor invoices, developer timesheets, and contemporaneous technical records for a minimum of six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
Furthermore, Budget 2024 enacted three major expansions to the CRA's statutory audit enforcement powers under the Income Tax Act that directly impact SR&ED technical and financial reviews:

items: Notice of Non-Compliance and Monetary Penalties: The CRA is now empowered to issue a formal "Notice of Non-Compliance" to any taxpayer that fails to comply fully with a CRA audit requirement or request for documentation or assistance, carrying an automatic monetary penalty ($50 per day up to $25,000) for as long as the notice remains outstanding.

Mandatory Questioning Under Oath or Affirmation: During an audit, the CRA now holds the statutory authority to require that any oral or written information, technical explanations, or documentation be provided under oath or solemn affirmation (by affidavit or formal examination under oath). This allows CRA Research and Technology Advisors and auditors to examine lead engineers, CTOs, and corporate officers under oath regarding the accuracy of their timesheets and technical narratives.

Tolling of the Assessment Limitation Period: Budget 2024 amended the assessment limitation period rules so that the statutory "normal reassessment period" clock is automatically suspended ("stopped") during any period in which a Notice of Non-Compliance is outstanding or during any judicial review of a CRA compliance requirement.

body.text: 8. Strategic Recommendations and Audit Defence Blueprint

To maximize non-dilutive recovery under the enacted Bill C-15 framework while insulating claims against the CRA's expanded audit powers, Canadian enterprises and their tax advisors should implement a cohesive, five-part compliance strategy.

First, scaling technology, life sciences, and industrial enterprises should immediately recalibrate their capital and corporate structures for the enacted Bill C-15 thresholds applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital of up to $15 million now qualify for the enhanced 35% refundable rate on up to $6.0 million of annual expenditures (up to $2.1 million in cash refunds), with a reduced expenditure limit continuing up to $75 million, and venture-backed CCPCs carrying high debt or preferred share capital on their balance sheets should model the new three-year average revenue election to avoid taxable-capital phase-out grinds. Similarly, Canadian-resident public companies not controlled by non-residents should claim the 35% refundable credit as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), while all claimants acquiring dedicated R&D hardware, GPUs, or lab apparatus after December 15, 2024, should capture the reinstated subsection 37(1)(b) capital expenditure credit alongside the 100% immediate CCA expensing rules for Classes 44, 46, and 50 (for assets acquired between April 16, 2024, and December 31, 2026).

Second, finance teams must perform rigorous arithmetic modelling between the 55% Proxy Method and the Traditional Method rather than defaulting to the proxy election. Claimants must verify that the Prescribed Proxy Amount is calculated at the statutory 55% rate under ITR subsection 2900(4) (never the obsolete pre-2013 65% rate) and ensure that no overhead cloud computing costs are claimed on top of the 55% PPA. Where a compute-intensive AI or data-engineering team's unsubsidized experimental cloud infrastructure spend exceeds 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base, electing the Traditional Method—supported by strict AWS/Azure/GCP resource tagging that isolates experimental R&D clusters from production COGS—unlocks substantial incremental tax credits.

Third, corporations with 10%+ founder-shareholders (specified employees) must proactively structure executive compensation as fixed T4 base salary paid prior to fiscal year-end. Because ITR subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) strip bonuses, profit-based remuneration, stock options, and subsection 78(4) unpaid wages out of a specified employee's SR&ED salary base and cap their PPA salary base at the lesser of 75% of total base salary and 2.5 times the YMPE, shifting founder compensation from year-end bonuses to regular base payroll directly expands both direct wage eligibility and the 55% notional overhead proxy.

Fourth, multi-provincial enterprises must harmonize their internal cost tracking with the 2025–2026 provincial reforms, particularly in Québec, Ontario, and Alberta. In Québec, companies whose fiscal periods begin after March 25, 2025, must transition from the repealed RD-1029.7 wage credit to the new Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), establishing general ledger accounts to capture newly eligible downstream pre-commercialization expenses and R&D capital equipment at the 30% and 20% refundable rates. In Ontario, claimants must apply the sequential OITC (8%) and ORDTC (3.5%) assistance grinds accurately and include post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures on Schedule 566, while AI builders nationwide should stack the AI Compute Access Fund (66.67% domestic compute cost-share) and NRC IRAP with SR&ED by separating compute line items from engineering payroll and cross-disclosing all assistance on Form T661.

Finally, to defend the 96% claim approval rate against the Federal Court of Appeal's strict Question-5 jurisprudence (Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2026 FCA 175; Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6) and the CRA's new Budget 2024 authority to compel testimony under oath or affirmation and issue $50/day Notices of Non-Compliance, engineering organizations must embed contemporaneous SR&ED documentation directly into their daily development workflows. By tagging Jira tickets, Git commits, experiment logs, quantitative test metrics, and developer timesheets in real time as hypotheses are formulated and tested, claimants establish an unassailable evidentiary record well ahead of the non-extendable 18-month statutory filing deadline under subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act.
